title: 106 Influence of timing of grazing during the growing season on forage utilization, foraging efficiency, botanical composition, and diet quality in semi-arid rangelands
content:
Abstract
Current grazing management recommendations for semi-arid rangeland include deferring grazing during the growing season to allow forage recovery from defoliation on an every other year or a two out of every three year basis. Though research supports that deferment during the growing season is fundamental to maintaining sustainable grazing systems, there is limited information available that investigates how grazing behavior changes throughout the growing season. Therefore, our objectives were to evaluate the impacts of timing of grazing during the growing season on diet quality, botanical composition of diet, and foraging behavior of beef cattle grazing on semi-arid, bunchgrass-dominated rangelands. In the late Spring through mid-Summer of 2024, cattle grazed 16 four hectare pastures arranged in a complete randomized block design (four blocks, each containing four pastures). Four treatments were randomly assigned within each block; 1) grazed in the early growing season (May 16-June 6), 2) grazed in the middle of the growing season (June 6-June 27), 3) grazed late in the growing season (June 27-July 18), and 4) ungrazed control pastures. At the initiation of each grazing treatment, six ruminally-evacuated cannulated cows were observed grazing for 20 minutes to collect bite counts by species and rumen samples to evaluate foraging behavior and diet composition. Clippings of both grasses and forbs were taken from each pasture pre- and post-grazing to assess forage utilization and pasture potential regrowth. For foraging behavior, g/min consumed differed among treatments (P< 0.01). In May, cattle consumed 7.42 g/min less than in early June (P< 0.01), but 8.72 g/min more than in late June (P< 0.01). Late June’s rate of consumption in g/min was lower in late June than all other time periods (P< 0.01). Additionally, bites/min displayed a quadratic relationship with timing of grazing (P=0.03), with the greatest bites/min early in the growing season, in contrast to later in the growing season. In contrast, g/bite increased linearly (P< 0.01) as the growing season progressed, ranging from 1.07 to 1.58 g/bite. Grass composition of diets decreased linearly (P< 0.01) as the growing season progressed, ranging from 94.39% in May to 52.34% in July. In contrast, forb composition of the diet increased linearly (P< 0.01) as the growing season progressed, ranging from 5.61% in May to 47.69% in July. In summary, grazing behavior and diet composition differed across time throughout the growing season. This suggests that as the season progresses, cattle alter their foraging strategy to optimize nutrient intake. Grass to forb ratios of the diet and foraging behavior, as a function of timing of grazing within the growing season, reflect these foraging strategies.
